title: Sampling Distribution
body:
**The idea block 3 turns on, and it is the conceptual jump of the course.** You took one sample and
computed $\bar{x}$. You could have taken a different sample and got a different $\bar{x}$. So
$\bar{X}$ is itself a [[Random Variable]], and it has a distribution of its own: the **sampling
distribution**.

Three distributions get confused constantly, so keep them apart:

| Distribution | Of what | Spread |
|---|---|---|
| Population | individual values in the world | $\sigma$ |
| Sample | the $n$ values you measured | $s$ |
| **Sampling distribution** | a *statistic*, over all possible samples | $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$ |

The third one is not something you ever observe. You take one sample, not thousands. It is a
theoretical object, and the entire value of inference is that theory tells you its shape without
your having to build it.

## Mean and standard error

For a simple random sample of size $n$:

$$
E[\bar{X}] = \mu, \qquad \text{SD}(\bar{X}) = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
$$

The first says $\bar{X}$ is **unbiased**: on average across samples it lands on the truth. The
second is derived in [[Variance]] from $\text{Var}(\bar{X}) = \sigma^2/n$, and it gets its own name,
the **standard error**, to keep it distinct from the population's $\sigma$.

**Standard error is the whole point.** $\sigma$ describes how much individuals vary and does not
shrink; $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$ describes how much your *estimate* varies and shrinks as you collect data.
Every error bar, every interval width, and every test statistic denominator in blocks 3 through 6 is
a standard error.

$$
\text{halving the error bar costs } 4\times \text{ the data}
$$

because of the square root. That is the most practically useful sentence in the course: it is why
polls stall at about 1000 respondents, and why the marginal value of more data falls off a cliff.

When $\sigma$ is unknown, which is nearly always, it is estimated by $s$ and the standard error
becomes $s/\sqrt{n}$. That substitution is what forces the $t$ distribution instead of $z$; see
[[Confidence Interval]].

## Point estimation

A **point estimator** is any statistic used to guess a parameter: $\bar{x}$ for $\mu$, $s^2$ for
$\sigma^2$, $\hat{p}$ for $p$. Two properties decide whether it is a good one.

- **Bias** is $E[\hat{\theta}] - \theta$, the systematic error. Unbiased means it is right on
  average. This is why [[Variance]] divides by $n - 1$: dividing by $n$ gives a biased estimator and
  the correction removes exactly that bias.
- **Standard error** is the random error, how much it bounces around.

They trade off, and being unbiased is not automatically better: an estimator that is slightly off
but very stable can beat one that is centred but wild. That trade has a name in
[[MACHINE LEARNING]], the **bias-variance trade-off**, and it is the same quantity being discussed.
An overfit model has low bias and high variance, exactly like an estimator computed from too little
data.

> [!note] Two different "bias"
> Statistical bias here means $E[\hat{\theta}] \neq \theta$, a property of an estimator. The **bias
> term** in a neuron ([[Bias Term]], [[Neural Network]]) is an additive parameter, and sampling bias
> in [[Descriptive Statistics]] is a flaw in how data was collected. Three unrelated things, one
> word.

## Where it goes

The sampling distribution's *shape* is still open at this point. It comes from the
[[Central Limit Theorem]], which says it is approximately normal for large $n$ whatever the
population looks like. Shape plus centre plus standard error is everything needed to build a
[[Confidence Interval]] or run a [[Hypothesis Testing|test]], and that is precisely the programme of
the rest of the course.

## Related

- [[Central Limit Theorem]]: the shape
- [[Confidence Interval]]: turning a standard error into a range
- [[Hypothesis Testing]]: turning one into a decision
- [[Variance]]: where $\sigma^2/n$ and the $n-1$ correction come from
- [[Stratification]]: stratified sampling, which reduces the standard error by sampling within
  homogeneous groups
